extracted.intended_audience: distance-education faculty, administrators, and practitioners implementing PLAR/e-portfolio systems (adult educators and assessors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating, managing, and assessing prior learning assessment and recognition (PLAR) portfolios — including stages of portfolio development, required parts, assessment methodology, online/e-portfolio issues, and institutional implementation in open and distance learning (ODL) contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of prior learning (UNESCO definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal acknowledgement of skills, knowledge, and competencies that are gained through work experience, informal training, and life experience (Vlãsceanu, Grünberg, & Pârlea, 2004, p. 55).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PLAR should honour and build on mature learners' past experiential learning; definitions and rationale (Dewey, Kolb) should inform practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of PLAR approach: challenge-for-credit vs portfolio assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: AU implements PLAR using both challenge-for-credit and portfolio assessment methods; challenge-for-credit targets specific courses while portfolio assessment permits broader demonstration of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge-for-credit requires tailoring learning histories to fit pre-determined course knowledge clusters; portfolio approach allows learners to demonstrate prior knowledge more fully and to build new knowledge through reflection, selection, connection, and projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio as vehicle for credit and lifelong learning (low-stakes vs high-stakes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolios serve as repositories of achievement and methods of celebrating growth (low-stakes) and as high-stakes assessment tools when submitted for university credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-stakes portfolios must provide rigorous evidence and are treated as performance-assessment instruments that can fast-track credentials; their stakes require stronger structures and supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required portfolio components (document structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire document should contain most of the following parts: table of contents, resume, narrative autobiography or personal narrative, chronological learning history, educational and career goals, demonstration of learning through learning statements, and documentation of learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portfolios are designed to triangulate learners' demonstration of knowledge; documentation often forms the bulkiest part and should support learning statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation and documentation of learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentation of learning often forms the bulkiest part of the portfolio and includes many types of documents, including letters of attestation written by externals to validate claims, and copies of credentials, awards, certificates, and other artefacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors expect corroborating artefacts to support learning statements; collect diverse evidence to triangulate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing learning statements (use Bloom's Taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning statements form the body of the demonstrated evidence of the learning that PLAR applicants claim to have achieved; based on Bloom’s Taxonomy (knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, evaluation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose statements reflecting appropriate cognitive levels; learners often struggle and need scaffolding. The writing process itself is a knowledge-construction exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: PLAR development stages: Reflect
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners start from personal meaning and relevance and engage in thoughtful reflection, moving from the mundane to a higher level of interpretation (Crites, 1971).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help learners elevate personal stories to more generic knowledge, identify lessons and skills embedded in experience (example: transforming household management into organizational skill claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: PLAR development stages: Select
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must mine their rich and varied experiences selectively for events that can most effectively anchor the learning narrative; selections act as scaffolding for the learning story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select incidents strategically to map histories and futures and to label them as valuable pieces of self-knowledge; be selective rather than exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: PLAR development stages: Connect
rubrics_metrics.description: Once knowledge items are identified they must be linked or arranged into an order that serves the purpose; connecting experience to meaning is central (Kolb, situated cognition, transformation theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use learning cycles (participation → meaning making → application → action → feedback) and critical reflection to create coherent narratives and demonstrate knowledge-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: PLAR development stages: Project (presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must determine an appropriate presentation method to project evidence in a format acceptable to the receiving institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conforming to structured expectations satisfies generic/process outcomes (accurate document construction, appropriate textual communication, understanding/adapting learning style). Choose formats that enable assessors to see the learning story clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic/process outcomes from portfolio preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Process outcomes might be labelled: using and constructing documents accurately; communicating appropriately in text; understanding one’s learning style; and adapting it to tasks at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achievement of these outcomes is part of the learning demonstrated by preparing a portfolio; they should be addressed explicitly in guidance to applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portfolio as knowledge-building (portfolio-as-journey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolio development is analogized as a journey with meandering, false starts, surprises and difficulties; cognitive engagement with learning histories gives rise to new knowledge of self and profession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the portfolio process as a learning activity that fosters transformational learning and reflexivity; design supports accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment rigor for high-stakes PLAR
rubrics_metrics.description: To persuade critics, PLAR systems must demonstrate a system that is rigorous, sound, and capable of initiating self-reflection and critical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return to first principles (value experiential learning, constructivist approaches) and ensure criteria, procedures, and assessor training convey credibility and defensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment methodology constraints in ODL (text-based emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distance institutions limit choice of assessment methods (ruling out interviews or performance displays); Athabasca uses only portfolio assessment, increasing importance of text-based abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design portfolios and supports with strong emphasis on written communication, clarity of learning statements, and alternate media where feasible; be explicit about acceptable evidence types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication: iterative format and high-quality resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Helping applicants grapple with the extent and value of past learning is best accomplished via an iterative format that allows reflection to evolve (Schön, 1987); ODL environments require well-developed structure and responsive communication systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide continual application of written/verbal skills, high-quality resources (paper & online), and mechanisms for iterative feedback (mentoring, coaching, email, telephone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support services for PLAR learners
rubrics_metrics.description: Support takes many forms: advising, counselling, coaching, mentoring, technology/web support; communities of practice and peer support are important; human interaction via phone and email is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer both material (resources, templates, virtual portfolio examples) and human supports; PLAR learner support should resemble course-oriented learner support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources and access modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide both paper-based and online resources; virtual portfolios allow near-hands-on access; different learners prefer different modalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure multiple access channels (paper, web, virtual examples) to honour access principles and learner preferences; expect gradual increase in digital-native comfort over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-portfolio: risk of privileging form over content (Focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: The e-portfolio draws on multimedia development and portfolio development; concern exists that emphasis on software design will lessen learners' attention to content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design e-portfolio guidance to prioritize evidence of learning and reflection; set expectations that multimedia/technical features should enhance, not overshadow, learning stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-portfolio: assessment equity and assessor alienation
rubrics_metrics.description: E-portfolio technology may alienate assessors and shift attention away from content; some faculty prefer paper due to increased computer usage required by e-portfolios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train assessors in evaluating e-portfolios, provide neutral rubrics and exemplars, and ensure technology does not create bias against certain learners or advantage others unfairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and technology-mediated inequities
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing technology privileges some learners above others; paper platforms also disadvantage others—access is not a level playing field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider differential access and digital literacy; provide alternatives and scaffolding to avoid exacerbating inequities when implementing e-portfolios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical fit: learner ownership and constructivist approach
rubrics_metrics.description: E-portfolios (and portfolios in general) should be student-owned and student-centred, enabling active engagement consistent with constructivist theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage learner control, reflection, and knowledge construction; balance learner choice with institutional accountability for high-stakes credit decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional/operational structure for PLAR
rubrics_metrics.description: Athabasca University maintains a central office where personnel champion, direct, and manage the PLAR process; such internal and integrated structure supports coherent, institution-wide PLAR policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement centralized coordination (champions, offices, integrated policies) to ensure consistent procedures, communications, and assessor practices across programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative mentoring/coaching is preferred where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Face-to-face or iterative mentoring/coaching best supports the complex cognitive work of portfolio preparation; distributed environments must replicate iterative feedback via other channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where interviews/performances are not possible, build iterative written/email/telephone feedback loops, peer groups, and coaching to approximate mentoring interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessor fairness and 'who controls knowledge' concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Portfolio assessment raises questions of power/voice: Who controls knowledge? Can academic faculty fairly assess portfolio learning?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop transparent criteria, training, and appeals processes; involve external attestations and multiple forms of evidence to reduce assessor bias and contestation.
